arrangement.rule: Start with 16-32 bars of beat before anything melodic.
arrangement.why: A DJ needs a plain section to mix into. A track that starts on the drop is unmixable and gets skipped.

arrangement.rule: Every section is a multiple of 8 bars, usually 16 or 32.
arrangement.why: Dancers and DJs both count in 8s. A 12-bar section lands wrong and no one can tell you why.

arrangement.rule: The first drop belongs 20-40% into the track.
arrangement.why: Earlier and there is no tension to release. Later and the floor drifts.

arrangement.rule: A drop needs a quieter section before it.
arrangement.why: Loudness is relative. Without contrast the ear stops registering loud.

arrangement.rule: Change one element per 8 or 16 bars, not three.
arrangement.why: Techno is about noticing a single change. Three at once reads as chaos.

arrangement.rule: Peak energy minus minimum energy should exceed 0.4.
arrangement.why: A flat track is a long loop. The shape is the composition.

arrangement.rule: End with 16-32 bars of thinning beat.
arrangement.why: Same reason as the intro, in reverse: the next DJ needs somewhere to go.

arrangement.rule: The main motif should appear in at least three sections.
arrangement.why: Repetition is what makes a track memorable. A new idea every section is eight loops, not a song.

dj.rule: Start a blend on a phrase boundary, not a bar boundary.
dj.why: Phrases are 16 or 32 bars. Landing mid-phrase makes both tracks feel wrong.

dj.rule: Never run two basslines at once. Swap the lows at the midpoint.
dj.why: Two sub sources double the energy in the one band with no headroom.

dj.rule: Mix within one step on the Camelot wheel.
dj.why: Two keys a tritone apart beat against each other audibly.

dj.rule: Mix into equal or higher energy across a set.
dj.why: A set is one arrangement at a larger scale. The same rules apply.
Past that, drums start to sound obviously time-stretched.

bass.note: Sits above the kick. Highpass at ~60Hz to stay out of it.

clap.note: 1-2kHz is where a clap reads as a clap.

hat.note: Above 8k. Below that it fights the mids.

oh.note: Longer than a closed hat, so it masks more. Use sparingly.

pad.note: Wide and long, so it masks everything. Duck it or filter it.

perc.note: The band with the most room in most techno tracks.

rumble.note: Sits under the kick and fills the gap between hits. Sidechain it or it eats the kick.

sub.note: Conflicts with the kick by definition. Sidechain hard or write it to play in the kick's gaps.

acid.note: The 303 is the lead, the hook and the arrangement. Move the filter, not the notes.

ambient.note: A drop here is a tide, not a cliff. Chords carry the track and the drums are weather.

breakbeat.note: The break IS the hook. Keep the kick off the grid and let the snare drag - straight sixteenths would kill it.

downtempo.note: Head-nod music. The kick lands late and heavy; the air between hits does half the work.

dubtechno.note: Chords through long delays. Nothing arrives suddenly.

electro.note: Machine funk: syncopated kick under a straight hat. The bassline talks; everything else answers it.

garage.note: Two-step: the kick skips beat three and the shuffle is the groove. If it sounds straight, it is wrong.

hardtechno.note: Distorted kick carries the track. Rumble tails fill the gaps between kicks - that smear IS the genre.

house.note: Swing is the whole feel. Straight house is broken house.

industrial.note: Metallic percussion and noise. Ugly on purpose, tight anyway.

jungle.note: The break dances on top; the sub walks underneath at half speed. Two tempos in one track, and both must groove.

minimal.note: Space is an instrument. What you leave out is the composition.

psytrance.note: The rolling offbeat bass IS the track - a sixteenth-note machine that never stops. Everything else decorates it.

techno.note: Hypnotic and mechanical. Repetition is the point; change one element at a time and let it ride.

trance.note: The breakdown is the song. Everything before it is setup.

laid.why: Behind the beat. Dub and the deeper end sit here; it feels heavier without being slower.

pushed.why: Everything but the downbeat lands fractionally early. Reads as urgency, and it is why hard techno feels faster than its BPM.

straight.why: Dead on the grid. The accent curve alone gives it shape, which is what techno wants - the machine is the point.

swung.why: The offbeat sixteenth arrives late. This is the shuffle house is built on, and straight house is broken house.

mixing.rule: Duck the bass 6dB or more against the kick.
mixing.why: They occupy the same band. Ducking is what lets both be loud.

mixing.rule: Highpass anything that is not the kick above ~60Hz.
mixing.why: Sub energy from three sources sums to mud and eats all the headroom.

mixing.rule: One element owns each band at any moment.
mixing.why: Masking is inaudible as a problem and obvious as a result.
Clipping on a limiter is distortion you cannot undo later.
Wide bass cancels on a mono club system - the one place it must not.

BANDS:

  rumble 30-120Hz: Sits under the kick and fills the gap between hits. Sidechain it or it eats the kick.

  bass 60-400Hz: Sits above the kick. Highpass at ~60Hz to stay out of it.
  stab 300-3000Hz: Mid-range hook.
  clap 1000-3000Hz: 1-2kHz is where a clap reads as a clap.
  snare 180-4000Hz: Body at 180, snap at 2k.
  hat 8000-16000Hz: Above 8k. Below that it fights the mids.

clap_on_3.why: Backbeat on beats 2 and 4. Borrowed from rock and it still works, because the ear expects it.

four_floor.why: A kick on every beat gives every other element a grid. It is the reason techno is danceable at any tempo.

offbeat_bass.why: Bass in the kick's gaps means no sidechain is needed - they never collide in the first place.

offbeat_hat.why: A hat between kicks doubles the perceived tempo without changing the BPM. This is why house feels faster than it is.

rolling_16ths.why: Constant 16ths on a closed hat is momentum with no information. Vary the accents or it is wallpaper.

tresillo.why: 3-3-2. The most common syncopation on earth, and it makes a straight 4/4 groove immediately.

why.ab: A/B stores the current session in a slot, then swaps it back on the next call - a quick way to compare two versions and pick the one that's actually better.
why.accent: An accent - capital X in a pattern, or ! after a note - hits louder and sharper than a normal step. It's how a flat 16 steps gets a pulse: ears lock onto the loud ones and the pattern starts to groove instead of just ticking.
why.air: 8000-20000Hz - shimmer and openness. Open hats and cymbal wash live here. Too little sounds shut in a box; too much sounds thin and hissy.
why.bandpass: Bandpass only lets a narrow window of frequencies through, cutting above and below. It's a telephone/radio effect - thin and focused. Good for a stab you want to sit in one spot without fighting anything else.
why.bass: 60-250Hz - low-mid weight and warmth, where basslines live. Together with sub, this is the band that turns to mud fastest when kick and bass overlap - what sidechain and highpass are for.
why.bpm: BPM is the tempo - beats per minute, one beat per quarter note. Techno usually lives 125-145; higher feels relentless, lower feels heavier and more spacious.
why.clipping: Clipping is the signal trying to go louder than 0dB and getting flattened instead - it sounds harsh and crackly. If the master meter is pinned red, turn something down, usually the loudest track's gain, not everything at once.
why.cutoff: Cutoff is the frequency where the filter starts working. Raise it on a lowpass and the sound gets brighter, more top end let through; lower it and it gets darker, muffled. It's the one knob that turns a static pattern into a filter sweep - sweep it slowly and the whole room feels it build.
why.decay: Decay is how fast a sound dies away after it's triggered. Short = tight and clicky (closed hats, techno kicks); long = washy and sustained (open hats, pads). The difference between a knock and a ring.
why.euclidean: A euclidean rhythm spreads N hits as evenly as possible across a pattern's steps - the same maths that makes clock gears mesh evenly. It's why 5 hits against 16 steps still feels danceable instead of random: they're spaced as evenly as 5 can go into 16.
why.filter: Filter shapes tone by cutting frequencies above (lowpass), below (highpass), or both sides of (bandpass) the cutoff. `filter bass lp 420 res 0.8` is a lowpass at 420Hz, fairly resonant.
why.fx: Fx chains an effect onto a track (or `master` for the whole mix) - `fx bass drive amount 2.5` adds drive; `fx bass off` clears it. Stacks with the track's own filter, applied after it.
why.fxlist: Lists every effect currently registered - everything you can chain on with `fx`.
why.gain: Gain is a track's volume, a plain multiplier. 1.0 is unity, lower turns it down, higher turns it up - but watch the master meter, pushing several tracks past 1.0 is how you clip.
why.gen: Generates a starting pattern (acid/techno/minimal) so you're never starting from silence - a sketch to edit, not a final answer.
why.headroom: Headroom is the gap between how loud you're playing and 0dB, where things clip. Keep a few dB of it - mix a bit under full scale - so accents and buildups have somewhere to go without distorting.
why.highpass: Highpass is the opposite: lets the highs through, cuts everything below the cutoff. Use it to carve room out of a low end - `filter bass hp 100` removes the mud below 100Hz so the kick has the sub to itself.
why.humanize: Humanize adds small random timing jitter, in ms, to every hit, so the pattern isn't robotically exact. A little (2-5ms) feels loose and human; a lot starts to sound drunk. Zero is a machine - techno often wants the machine.
why.load: Reads a .thud file and replays its commands to rebuild that exact session.
why.low-mid: 250-800Hz - body and honk. Boxy or congested if this band gets crowded; clashing pads and stabs usually fight here.
why.lowpass: Lowpass lets the lows through and rolls off everything above the cutoff. It's the muffled-to-bright knob: closed cutoff sounds like it's behind a wall, open cutoff lets it breathe. The classic acid/techno filter.
why.mid: 800-2500Hz - where most instruments and vocals sit, and where the ear is most sensitive. Small changes here are loud changes.
why.mute: Mute silences a track completely without losing its pattern - flip it back on any time. Good for building a track up piece by piece.
why.notes: Notes are the pitches a melodic track (bass/stab) plays per step, e.g. `a1 . a1~ c2!` - note name, ~ to slide from the previous note, ! to accent.
why.open: Loads a song by name from songs/ (or a full .thud path), replacing the current session.
why.pan: Pan moves a track left/right in the stereo field. -1 is hard left, 0 centre, 1 hard right. Spreading tracks out gives everything room instead of piling up in the middle.
why.pattern: A pattern is characters, any length: x = hit, X = accent (louder), . or - = rest. Any length works - a 5-step pattern against a 16-step kick is a polymeter for free.
why.play: Play/stop starts and stops the transport. thud always keeps looping the current bar; play just starts the loop.
why.polymeter: Polymeter is two patterns of different lengths looping at the same time - a 5-step bassline against a 16-step kick, say. They only realign every 80 steps, so the same two patterns keep sounding like new combinations. thud gives you this for free: just make a track's pattern a different length.
why.presence: 2500-8000Hz - bite and attack, the band that cuts through a club system. Hats and claps live up here; too much gets harsh and fatiguing.
why.rec: Starts or stops recording exactly what you hear to a .wav in takes/, plus a .thud alongside it so the same session can be reloaded or handed to anyone.
why.redo: Steps forward again after an undo.
why.render: Renders the current pattern offline to a .wav without needing to play it live - useful for quick exports.
why.resonance: Resonance boosts the frequencies right at the cutoff before the filter rolls them off. Low (0.2-0.4) just softens the edge. High (0.8+) makes the filter ring at the cutoff - that ringing IS the acid squelch. Push it past ~0.9 on a lowpass and it starts to self-oscillate, almost singing on its own.
why.save: Writes the current session - tempo, patterns, every command that shaped it - to a .thud file you can reload later or hand to someone.
why.sidechain: Sidechain ducks a track's volume every time the kick hits, then lets it back up before the next one. It's the pumping techno sound, and practically it's how kick and bass share the same low end without turning to mud. `sidechain bass 0.7` ducks bass by 70% on every kick.
why.slide: A slide - ~ after a note - glides the pitch from the previous note into this one instead of jumping. It's the wet, vocal-ish glide in acid basslines; the 303 sound is basically slides plus resonance.
why.solo: Solo silences every other track so you hear just this one. Good for checking a sound is clean before bringing it back into the mix.
why.songs: Lists the starter songbook in songs/ - ready-made templates to load and learn from or build on top of.
why.stop: Stops playback. The pattern is still there, ready to resume from the top of the bar.
why.sub: 20-60Hz - sub bass. Felt more than heard on small speakers; kick and bass fundamentals live here. Too much and a mix sounds boomy on a real system.
why.swing: Swing delays every other 16th step, so the groove limps instead of marching in a straight grid. 0% is dead straight (hard techno); 15-25% starts to feel like a shuffle; much higher gets drunk and lopsided fast.
why.track: Track adds or removes a track - thud isn't fixed at 8. `track add rumble sub` adds one called rumble playing the sub voice; `track del rumble` removes it.
why.tune: Tune sets a voice's pitch or tone centre. On a melodic track (bass/stab) it's the base note; on a noise-based track (hat/perc) it shifts the whole timbre brighter or darker.
why.undo: Steps back one edit. Every pattern or parameter change is undoable, so mistakes are free.
why.variation: Mutates a couple of steps in a pattern at random - a quick way to keep a loop moving without hand-editing every step.
why.view: View switches which panel fills the middle of the screen - pattern grid, spectrum, scope, whatever's registered. perform is always there.
why.voice: Voice points a track at a different sound engine - same pattern, same steps, different instrument underneath. `voice bass reese` swaps the 303 for a reese bass.
why.voices: Lists every sound engine currently registered - everything you can point a track at with `voice`.
